title: IUPAC Classification and Periodic Trends
topicTitle: IUPAC classification of elements; periodic trend and periodicity: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters
notes: **IUPAC group numbering:** Groups 1–18, numbered left to right. This replaced the old European system (IA–VIIIA, IB–VIIIB) and American system (A/B). The IUPAC system is now the universal standard. Group 1 = alkali metals; Group 2 = alkaline earth metals; Group 17 = halogens; Group 18 = noble gases.

**Atomic radius — definition and measurement:** The atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together (covalent radius for non-metals, metallic radius for metals, van der Waals radius for noble gases). For example, in Cl$_2$, the Cl–Cl bond length is 198 pm, so the covalent radius of Cl is 99 pm.

**Atomic radius trend across a period:** Decreases from left to right. As Z increases across a period, electrons are added to the same shell while protons are added to the nucleus. The effective nuclear charge (Z$_{eff}$) increases, pulling the electron cloud closer. Example (Period 3): Na (186 pm) > Mg (160 pm) > Al (143 pm) > Si (117 pm) > P (110 pm) > S (104 pm) > Cl (99 pm) > Ar (71 pm, van der Waals).

**Atomic radius trend down a group:** Increases from top to bottom. Each successive element adds a new electron shell (higher n), which increases the distance of valence electrons from the nucleus. Shielding by inner electrons increases, so Z$_{eff}$ on valence electrons changes little. Example (Group 1): Li (152 pm) < Na (186 pm) < K (227 pm) < Rb (248 pm) < Cs (265 pm).

**Ionic radius — cations:** Cations are smaller than their parent atoms because losing electrons reduces electron–electron repulsion and the remaining electrons are pulled closer by the same nuclear charge. Na (186 pm) → Na$^+$ (102 pm) — a 45% reduction. Mg (160 pm) → Mg$^{2+}$ (72 pm). The loss of an entire shell (e.g., Na → Na$^+$ loses the 3s electron, leaving only n=1 and n=2) causes particularly large reductions.

**Ionic radius — anions:** Anions are larger than their parent atoms because added electrons increase electron–electron repulsion in the valence shell, causing it to expand. Cl (99 pm) → Cl$^-$ (181 pm). O (66 pm) → O$^{2-}$ (140 pm). The increase can be dramatic — O$^{2-}$ is more than double the radius of neutral O.

**Ionic radius trend within isoelectronic series:** For species with the same number of electrons, radius decreases as nuclear charge (Z) increases. Example (10 electrons): O$^{2-}$ (140 pm) > F$^-$ (133 pm) > Ne (not applicable) > Na$^+$ (102 pm) > Mg$^{2+}$ (72 pm) > Al$^{3+}$ (54 pm). More protons pull the same number of electrons closer.

**Ionization energy (IE):** The minimum energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) → X$^+$ (g) + e$^-$. First ionization energy (IE$_1$) is for removing the first electron. Second IE (IE$_2$) is for removing a second electron from X$^+$. IE always increases (IE$_1$ < IE$_2$ < IE$_3$) because each successive electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.

**IE trend across a period:** Increases from left to right. Higher Z$_{eff}$ holds electrons more tightly. Example (Period 3): Na (496 kJ/mol) < Mg (738) < Al (578) < Si (786) < P (1012) < S (1000) < Cl (1251) < Ar (1520). Note the exceptions: Al < Mg (removing from 3p vs 3s), S < P (electron–electron repulsion in paired 3p orbital).

**IE trend down a group:** Decreases from top to bottom. Valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are easier to remove. Example (Group 1): Li (520) > Na (496) > K (419) > Rb (403) > Cs (376) kJ/mol. This explains why alkali metals become more reactive down the group.

**Ionization energy and metallic character:** Low ionization energy means an element readily loses electrons — a characteristic of metals. High ionization energy means an element holds its electrons tightly — characteristic of non-metals. Fluorine (IE = 1681 kJ/mol) is the most non-metallic; cesium (IE = 376 kJ/mol) is the most metallic (excluding Fr).

**Electron affinity (EA):** The energy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) + e$^-$ → X$^-$ (g). By convention, a negative EA means energy is released (exothermic, favourable). Chlorine has the most negative EA (-349 kJ/mol) — it 'wants' an electron the most. Fluorine (-328 kJ/mol) is less than chlorine because its small size causes electron–electron repulsion in the compact 2p subshell.

**EA trend across a period:** Becomes more negative (more energy released) from left to right, generally. Non-metals have more negative EAs because they are closer to a stable noble gas configuration. Halogens have the most negative EAs (Group 17). Noble gases have positive EAs (energy must be added) because the added electron must enter a new, higher-energy shell.

**EA trend down a group:** Becomes less negative (less energy released) from top to bottom, with exceptions. Larger atoms can accommodate an extra electron with less repulsion, but the increased distance from the nucleus weakens the attraction. The anomaly F < Cl (in magnitude) is the classic exception, explained by F's small size causing high electron–electron repulsion.

**Electronegativity (EN):** The ability of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of bonding electrons toward itself. It is a relative, dimensionless property (not directly measurable for isolated atoms). The Pauling scale is most common: F = 3.98 (assigned as the highest), O = 3.44, N = 3.04, Cl = 3.16, C = 2.55, H = 2.20. The Allred–Rochow and Mulliken scales provide alternative definitions.

**EN trend across a period:** Increases from left to right, correlating with increasing Z$_{eff}$ and decreasing atomic radius. A more compact atom with higher nuclear charge attracts bonding electrons more strongly. This is why B–F bonds are highly polar (EN difference = 2.0) while C–H bonds are nearly non-polar (EN difference = 0.35).

**EN trend down a group:** Decreases from top to bottom, as atoms get larger and the bonding electrons are farther from the nucleus. This is why HF is a weak acid (strong H–F bond due to high EN of F) while HI is a strong acid (weak H–I bond).

**Metallic character:** The tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions. Metals are on the left and centre of the table; non-metals on the upper right. Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period. The most metallic element is cesium (or francium, though it is radioactive and rare). The most non-metallic is fluorine.

**Metallic character in reactions:** Metals undergo oxidation (lose electrons): Na → Na$^+$ + e$^-$. Non-metals undergo reduction (gain electrons): Cl + e$^-$ → Cl$^-$. The reactivity of metals correlates with low IE and low EN; the reactivity of non-metals correlates with high IE and high EN. Fluorine's extreme reactivity is due to its combination of highest EN, high EA, and weak F–F bond (159 kJ/mol).

**Periodicity of oxide character:** Metallic oxides are basic (Na$_2$O + H$_2$O → 2NaOH). Non-metallic oxides are acidic (CO$_2$ + H$_2$O → H$_2$CO$_3$). Amphoteric oxides (Al$_2$O$_3$, ZnO) react with both acids and bases, reflecting the intermediate position of Al and Zn in the periodic table. This trend correlates directly with electronegativity.

**Using periodic trends to predict properties:** Given an element's position, you can predict: (1) its metallic or non-metallic character, (2) the acidity/basicity of its oxide, (3) the type of bonds it forms (ionic with very different EN elements, covalent with similar EN), (4) the charge on its common ion, and (5) the strength of its bonds with hydrogen. These predictions are the practical power of periodicity.

**Nuclear charge vs. shielding:** The effective nuclear charge Z$_{eff}$ = Z - S, where Z is the actual nuclear charge and S is the shielding (screening) constant. Slater's rules provide a method for estimating S. Across a period, S increases slowly (only same-shell electrons shield poorly), so Z$_{eff}$ increases significantly. Down a group, S increases almost as fast as Z, so Z$_{eff}$ changes little — the size increase dominates.

Periodic trends are not isolated facts — they are interconnected consequences of one principle: the balance between nuclear attraction and electron–electron repulsion, modulated by quantum mechanical shell structure. Mastering Z$_{eff}$ unlocks all trends simultaneously.
confusion: Electron affinity vs. electronegativity: EA is a measurable energy change for an isolated atom gaining an electron (kJ/mol). EN is a relative, dimensionless scale describing an atom's pull on bonding electrons in a molecule. They correlate but are not the same thing — EN is about shared electrons; EA is about a completely gained electron.

Fluorine has the highest electronegativity but chlorine has the most negative electron affinity: F's small size causes intense electron–electron repulsion when an extra electron is added, making the process less favourable than for Cl. However, in a bond, F's small size and high Z allow it to attract shared electrons more strongly than Cl.

Ionization energy trend exceptions (Mg > Al, P > S): These occur because Mg has a stable 3s$^2$ configuration (removing from a filled s-orbital costs more) and P has a stable half-filled 3p$^3$ configuration. S has a paired 3p electron that is easier to remove due to electron–electron repulsion in the same orbital.

Ionic radius vs. atomic radius for the same element: Students often forget that cations are smaller and anions are larger. Na$^+$ (102 pm) is dramatically smaller than Na (186 pm), while Cl$^-$ (181 pm) is much larger than Cl (99 pm). The change is especially large when an entire electron shell is lost or gained.

Metallic character vs. reactivity: Metallic character (tendency to lose electrons) increases down a group, but reactivity of metals also involves bond energies and hydration energies. For example, Li has the highest IE in Group 1 yet is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution because of its very high hydration energy (due to small Li$^+$ size), not just its IE.
practice: Arrange the following in order of increasing atomic radius: S, O, Se, Te. Explain the trend using the concepts of principal quantum number and shielding. Then arrange their ionic radii (S$^{2-}$, O$^{2-}$, Se$^{2-}$, Te$^{2-}$) and explain why the ionic order mirrors the atomic order.

The first and second ionization energies of an element are 738 kJ/mol and 1451 kJ/mol, with a third IE of 7733 kJ/mol. (a) Which group does this element belong to? (b) What is its likely identity? (c) Explain the large jump between IE$_2$ and IE$_3$ in terms of electron configuration.

Explain why the electron affinity of fluorine (-328 kJ/mol) is less negative than that of chlorine (-349 kJ/mol), even though fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. In your answer, distinguish between the factors affecting EA (isolated atom) and EN (bonded atom).

Arrange Na$^+$, Mg$^{2+}$, F$^-$, O$^{2-}$ in order of increasing ionic radius. All are isoelectronic with 10 electrons. Explain your ordering using Z$_{eff}$ and show the nuclear charge for each species.

Element X is in Period 3, Group 15. (a) Write its electron configuration and identify the element. (b) Predict whether its oxide is acidic, basic, or amphoteric. (c) Compare its electronegativity with that of phosphorus and arsenic. (d) What is the formula of its hydride? Is it more or less stable than NH$_3$?
universalFacts: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (Pauling: 3.98). It forms compounds with every other element except helium, neon, and argon — including noble gas compounds like XeF$_2$ and H$_2$He$^+$ (the latter in extreme conditions).

The element with the highest first ionization energy is helium (2372 kJ/mol), not fluorine. Helium's 1s$^2$ electrons are closest to the nucleus with no shielding, making them the hardest to remove. Fluorine's IE is 1681 kJ/mol — the highest among elements with p-electrons.

The largest difference in electronegativity is between francium (~0.7) and fluorine (3.98), giving a difference of ~3.3. This produces the most ionic bond known (FrF). The smallest difference is between identical atoms (EN difference = 0), producing purely covalent bonds.

The concept of 'periodicity' means that properties repeat at regular intervals when elements are arranged by atomic number. The period length (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32) corresponds exactly to the capacity of successive electron subshells: 2, 2+6, 2+6, 2+10+6, 2+10+6, 2+14+10+6, 2+14+10+6.

Lanthanoid contraction (the gradual decrease in radii across the 4f series) causes the 4d and 5d transition series elements to have nearly identical radii. Zirconium (160 pm) and hafnium (159 pm) are virtually indistinguishable by size, making their separation by chemical means nearly impossible — they must be separated by fractional crystallization or ion exchange.
